query: For an equimolar WTaTiVZr high-entropy alloy made from low-activation refractory elements, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains its plastic strain and toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature mechanical loading relevant to sustained plasma-facing-component service? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations expected relative to pure tungsten, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The high configurational entropy in the equimolar WTaTiVZr high-entropy alloy leads to the formation of a solid-solution phase, which enhances its plastic strain and toughness under high-temperature mechanical loading compared to commercially used pure tungsten.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar WTaTiVZr high-entropy alloy in its as-cast state
generation.conditions: Temperature range: 873-1173 K, strain rate: 0.001-0.1 s^-1
generation.structural_mediator: Solid-solution phase with a single-phase BCC structure
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy in the alloy leads to the formation of a solid-solution phase, which enhances the alloy's resistance to dislocation movement and improves its plastic strain and toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: The equimolar WTaTiVZr high-entropy alloy will exhibit improved plastic strain and toughness compared to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature mechanical loading.
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 873-1173 K, strain rate: 0.001-0.1 s^-1
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism by which the high configurational entropy enhances the alloy's plastic strain and toughness is not fully understood and requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Uniaxial tensile tests on the equimolar WTaTiVZr high-entropy alloy and commercially used pure tungsten at various temperatures and strain rates.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the equimolar WTaTiVZr high-entropy alloy does not exhibit improved plastic strain and toughness compared to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature mechanical loading, the hypothesis is falsified.

concept of a high configurational entropy favoring the formation of a solid–solution phase, has recently attracted significant attention, and the resulting alloys are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) []. As a new class of metallic materials, HEAs or complicated concentrated alloys made up of four or more primary elements greatly increase the alloy design space [,,]. HEA microstructures can be tailored to suit desired qualities, including single-phase solid solution HEAs [,,] and HEAs with hierarchical microstructures [,,,]. Moreover, over a wide temperature range, an increasing number of appealing features in HEAs have been revealed, including an outstanding strength–ductility synergy at ambient temperature [,], extraordinary mechanical capabilities at cryogenic temperatures [], and ultrahigh strength at extreme temperatures [].
Refractory HEAs (RHEAs) stand out among various types of HEAs due to their unparalleled mechanical properties at high temperatures exceeding 800 °C, and even up to 1500 °C in some cases [,], making them viable options for high-temperature structural applications, outperforming typical Ni-based superalloys. The as-cast metal ingots were prepared by vacuum arc melting; all the used raw material elements had a high purity (>99.9 atomic percent, at%). Prior to arc-melting the raw materials, the residual oxygen in the arc-melter chamber was absorbed using a high-purity Ti-getter. The chemical composition of the metal ingots was NbTaHfTiZrV0.5. All ingots were flipped over and remelted more than 5–8 times to promote the homogeneity. The specific composition of the alloy is shown in Table 1. The weight of as-cast samples was 30 g. In addition, the effect of a 50% cold rolling on dendrites could be found. The size of the dendrites was clearly not uniform, and the size of the largest was dozens of times that of the smallest. The tensile stress–strain curves of the NbTaTiZrV0.5 RHEA at room temperature (RT) and high temperature (673–1273 K) are presented in Figure 4a. The tensile properties of this HEA were shown to be in agreement with a previous study []. At room temperature, the cold-rolled alloy showed excellent tensile properties, with a yield strength approaching 1200 MPa and a plasticity reaching 8%. When the temperature reached 673 K, the strain–stress curve revealed a serrated flow behavior at a constant strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1, while the strength decreased, and the plasticity increased greatly. This occurred mainly in the softening phase, which may be related to the reason for the improvement in the plasticity []. When the temperature increased further, the yield strength and plasticity of the alloy decreased stably, but the decreasing range was small. The yield strength decreased significantly, and the plasticity rose to more than 30% when the temperature increased to 1223 K.

The differentials between the UTS and YS were about 100 MPa, and gradually widened as the temperature rose. Work hardening appeared in all curves from RT to 1073 K. We speculated that this was due to the fact that the heat treatment did not completely eliminate the residual stress of the alloy after cold rolling [,]. In order to prove this, the rolled samples were analyzed by transmission electron microscopy before a tensile test (see Figure 5). Some obvious dense dislocation bands were found in Figure 5a, and in addition, the diffraction pattern indicated that the alloy retained the structure of a single-phase BCC after the prior treatment. The region where the dislocation band was located was enlarged to further analyze its composition. In Figure 5b, it can be clearly found that the previously thought dislocation band was composed of two rows of dislocations. After a further enlargement, it was found that each dislocation band was composed of dense, short dislocations. This proved the previous conjecture that the residual dislocation after cold rolling caused a work hardening of the alloy.
